item.title: University pays professor $600K after being punished for parodying land acknowledgments
item.description: Stuart Reges parodied the University of Washington's land acknowledgment on his syllabus, triggering censorship and a nearly yearlong investigation.
item.content:encoded:
The University of Washington has paid a professor $600,000 after punishing him for parodying a land acknowledgment in his syllabus.

Stuart Reges, a non-tenured computer science and engineering teaching professor at the university, said in his complaint that in September 2020, university officials encouraged professors (but did not require) to include the university's land acknowledgment statement in their class syllabus. Land acknowledgments are statements commonly used by universities and public institutions to recognize Native American tribes as the original inhabitants of the land on which campuses now sit.

Reges parodied the university's land acknowledgment in his Computer Programming II class syllabus in January 2022. Instead of using the university's land acknowledgment, he wrote, "I acknowledge that by the labor theory of property the Coast Salish people can claim historical ownership of almost none of the land currently occupied by the University of Washington."

The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) said that Reges was punished for his actions.

"UW was not amused. University officials censored Reges’ parody statement from his syllabus and created a competing class, so students could choose not to take a computer science class from Reges. The university also initiated a nearly year-long investigation of Reges under an 'antiharassment" policy,'" the organization said.

WOKE STUNT GOES HORRIBLY WRONG AS MICHIGAN DEMS OPEN CONVENTION WITH BRUTAL ‘LAND ACKNOWLEDGMENT’

On Thursday, FIRE announced that Reges' legal battle had concluded with the settlement, following a Ninth Circuit ruling last December in his favor. Under the settlement, the university may take no further action against him over the parody statement.

Reges said in FIRE's press release, "I am deeply grateful to FIRE for this legal victory which will remind public universities that they are obligated to respect the First Amendment rights of their students, faculty, and staff."

He added, "More importantly, I hope that my protest can help reverse a decade-long trend towards ideological conformity in academia and help to convince them that instead of ‘protecting’ students from controversial ideas, they should be helping them to learn how to cope with disagreement. Only then can we heal the deep divisions that confront us today."

Gabe Walters, a FIRE attorney, told Fox News Digital: 

"Professor Reges parodied UW's land acknowledgment statement knowing doing so might cause offense, but his deeper purpose was to encourage his colleagues to see beyond their partisan perspectives and consider that others might disagree with them. Epistemic humility is necessary to test ideas, and there's no better place to put ideas to the test than our colleges and universities," Walters said.

CONTROVERSIAL STREAMER HASAN PIKER'S LECTURE AXED BY UNIVERSITY OF WASHINGTON AMID FREE SPEECH QUESTIONS

He added that the case could be better understood by looking at it from the angle of other hot-button issues.

"Consider the flip side of the coin: a state that bans professors from putting indigenous land acknowledgment statements in their syllabi also is putting its thumb improperly on the scale of public debate, and as a non-partisan organization dedicated to the freedom of speech and academic freedom, FIRE also would represent the hypothetical professor who wants to include a sincere land acknowledgment on their syllabi but is prohibited from doing so — just as we've challenged Florida's ‘Stop WOKE Act’ and Texas's campus ban on drag performances."

The University of Washington provided the following statement to Fox News Digital:

"The University of Washington maintains that we acted appropriately, and this settlement is in no way an admission of any wrongdoing. Given the Ninth Circuit’s 2-1 decision overturning the federal district court’s decision in favor of the University, a settlement agreement was the most reasonable option due to the attorney fees and costs that would have resulted from the Ninth’s Circuit’s decision. Prof. Reges has retained his faculty position and continued teaching throughout this process, and his status with the UW remains unchanged."

Fox News' Kristine Parks contributed to this report.

item.title: Trump is dismantling Iran’s war machine, but America still needs an endgame
item.description: Iran exploited U.S. fears of escalation for decades, but Trump's military pressure campaign is finally making asymmetry work both directions.
item.content:encoded:
For nearly half a century, the Islamic Republic of Iran taught Washington to fear confrontation more than Tehran feared attacking American interests. The regime sponsored terrorism, armed proxies, threatened international shipping and targeted U.S. forces while exploiting American fears of "escalation." President Donald Trump has begun to reverse that equation.

The latest strikes matter not simply because Iranian radar, air defenses and maritime assets have been destroyed, but because Washington is imposing a principle Tehran understands: aggression will expose and diminish its military power. For a theocracy that built regional influence by convincing adversaries that retaliation was more dangerous than accommodation, this fundamentally changes the balance of fear.

The latest confrontation in the Persian Gulf illustrates that change. U.S. Central Command said its Sept. 1 operation struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) air defenses, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites after attempted Iranian attacks on commercial shipping and U.S. service members. Tehran responded with missiles and drones aimed toward Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain.

TRUMP RETALIATES AFTER IRAN ATTACK AS EXPERT WARNS REGIME IS GROWING MORE DANGEROUS

The attacks demonstrate that Iran remains dangerous, but not strategically strong. Possessing missiles capable of inflicting damage is not the same as possessing the power to dictate a conflict’s outcome. Each attempt to rebuild its machinery of aggression creates new vulnerabilities for American intelligence and military power to exploit.

This is one of the most consequential achievements of current U.S. policy. For years, Tehran followed a favorable cycle: build military capabilities, use them directly or through proxies, absorb a limited response, wait for calls for "de-escalation" and rebuild. Washington mistook restraint for deterrence. But deterrence exists only when aggression reliably leaves an adversary worse off, and the Trump administration is restoring that principle. When the IRGC rebuilds radar, surveillance or other capabilities threatening American forces and international commerce, Washington need not accept their restoration. Tehran’s reconstructed assets can instead become new liabilities.

IRAN PROVES THAT IT MIGHT CHANGE ITS MILITARY LEADERS, BUT IT’S NOT CHANGING STRATEGY

Nowhere is this transformation more important than in the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Republic has long treated the Persian Gulf as a geopolitical hostage. Tehran never needed to defeat the U.S. Navy; it needed only to make this vital waterway dangerous enough to frighten shipping companies, insurers, energy markets and governments. Missiles, drones, mines and fast boats became instruments of economic coercion.

America is now challenging that blackmail by protecting shipping while degrading Iran’s maritime surveillance and offensive capabilities. The same geography that gives Tehran leverage also exposes the infrastructure on which its ability to threaten international commerce depends.

IRAN WARNS SHIPS OF 'FORCEFUL RESPONSE' AS US-BACKED HORMUZ ROUTE CHALLENGES TEHRAN'S GRIP

The economic dimension makes this pressure even more consequential. Iran depends heavily on energy revenue to sustain its security institutions, patronage networks and military ambitions. Restricting oil exports therefore constrains the financial ecosystem sustaining the regime’s coercive power. The reported American "tanker for tanker" policy sharpens that message.

If Tehran endangers commercial vessels and turns the Persian Gulf into a battlefield, it cannot assume its own maritime assets will remain insulated from the consequences. For decades, the Islamic Republic perfected asymmetric warfare by forcing others to bear costs it could avoid. Washington is finally making asymmetry work against Tehran.

IRAN LOSES KEY ECONOMIC LIFELINE IN MIDDLE EAST THAT TRUMP'S SANCTIONS COULDN'T REACH AS DEADLOCK PERSISTS

This deserves to be recognized as a long-overdue shift from managing Iranian aggression to degrading the machinery that makes it possible. The Islamic Republic is not a conventional government, occasionally pursuing objectionable policies. The IRGC, its terrorist proxies, intelligence networks, missile forces and ideological militias are central instruments of a system that has used terrorism and coercion as statecraft since 1979.

American policy failed when it imagined that concessions, negotiations or temporary agreements could transform that system. Current policy rests on a more realistic premise: a regime built around coercion must confront costs it cannot simply transfer to its victims.

IRAN IS NOT A NORMAL NATION YOU CAN MAKE DEALS WITH; IT’S A NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT

The danger now is stopping halfway. Military superiority can destroy capabilities, but it cannot define victory. America may demolish Iranian radars, cripple maritime forces and obstruct oil exports while leaving one strategic question unanswered: What happens if the Islamic Republic survives and rebuilds? Tehran understands that Western attention shifts, administrations change and diplomacy returns.

Given time, a weakened regime can reconstruct weapons and networks, presenting a future president with the familiar choice between confrontation and another supposedly historic negotiation. Tactical success without a political endgame could ultimately recreate the problem America is now paying heavily to solve.

TRUMP HAS 3 CHOICES TO DEFINE VICTORY IF HE WANTS TO BEAT IRAN. NONE OF THEM ARE EASY

The endgame should not be an American invasion, occupation or nation-building project. Iran does not need America to invent a nation for it. It is an ancient country with a powerful national identity, an educated population and a political history extending far beyond the clerical regime established in 1979.

Nor should Washington empower separatist forces whose ambitions could turn regime collapse into state collapse. A fragmented Iran of more than 90 million people would be a catastrophe for Iranians and a strategic nightmare for America. Washington should seek to end the Islamic Republic’s capacity for terrorism and regional coercion while preserving Iran’s territorial integrity and continuity.

IRAN’S REGIME WON’T NEGOTIATE IN GOOD FAITH. TRUMP MUST BREAK ITS GRIP

A successful American endgame should envision a united Iran where clerical repression is dismantled, a security vacuum is prevented and Iranians can establish a secular, democratic political order. America should not select Iran’s future government, but preserving the Iranian state while the Islamic Republic disappears is profoundly in the U.S. national interest.

That requires looking beyond the next missile exchange. Military, economic and intelligence pressure must reinforce a coherent political strategy, ensuring that the regime cannot simply survive the current confrontation and rebuild the architecture of terrorism, proxy warfare and coercion that made it dangerous in the first place.

I'VE STUDIED MILITARY STRATEGY. TRUMP NOW FACES IRAN'S OLDEST BATTLEFIELD TRICK

The Islamic Republic remains capable of violence because the apparatus that has kept it alive has not disappeared. Its missiles and drones remain dangerous, its security organizations brutal and its rulers determined to use whatever instruments survive to project strength. But the strategic picture has changed.

Iran’s conventional military infrastructure has been badly damaged, its ability to dominate the Persian Gulf is being challenged, and the resources sustaining its power are under extraordinary pressure. Tehran’s retaliation should not intimidate Washington into abandoning a successful strategy. A wounded authoritarian regime often grows more violent precisely as its options narrow.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

For decades, American policymakers asked how much Iranian aggression Washington could absorb without triggering a wider confrontation. Trump has posed a better question: how much aggression can Tehran afford when every escalation puts more of its military and economic power at risk? That reversal may prove more consequential than any individual strike.

America is demonstrating that the world’s most aggressive state sponsor of Islamist terrorism cannot claim a permanent veto over regional security simply by threatening chaos whenever confronted. Washington should preserve the pressure, protect Iran’s territorial integrity, reject another premature diplomatic escape hatch and translate military superiority into a durable political outcome. Trump is breaking Iran’s war machine. This is no time to stop halfway.

item.title: Caitlin Clark not in Team USA's starting 5 for FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup opener vs China
item.description: Caitlin Clark began the FIBA Women's World Cup coming off the bench for Team USA, as Kara Lawson went with two veterans options, Chelsea Gray and Jackie Young, instead.
item.content:encoded:
For those who were excited to watch Caitlin Clark make her senior international debut with Team USA at the FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup on Friday against China, they had to wait just a bit to see her on the court.

Clark wasn’t featured in Kara Lawson’s starting five to start off the tournament against China, whom Team USA saw in the 2022 gold-medal game.

The starting guards for Team USA were Chelsea Gray and Jackie Young, while Breanna Stewart, Kahleah Copper and Napheesa Collier round out the group. Gray was a pivotal piece in the 2022 victory at the World Cup, but Young, despite being one of the best guards in the WNBA today, wasn’t on the squad.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Clark eventually checked in midway through the first quarter, as Team USA started to run up the scoreboard early on China, with Young scoring seven of the team’s first 20 points.

Clark finished the first quarter with a layup for two points, while dishing out four assists and notching a rebound.

Heading into the tournament, Lawson said that Clark has been "great" and "coachable."

WNBA STAR WILL MISS PLAYING IN FIBA WORLD CUP AFTER HER PASSPORT GOES MISSING IN THE MAIL

" I had my first experience with her this spring, I had never coached her before, been around her a ton before. She is just so competitive, skilled, sees the game at this high level in terms of her ability to be anticipatory, with her passes and with her shots, and her belief and confidence in what she can do is terrific," she said, per Sports Illustrated.

Clark was also coming into the tournament red-hot after setting multiple WNBA records in the month of August before this international break.

For starters, Clark scored or assisted on 44.7 points per game, a WNBA record for a single month. The stellar point guard has always had a knack for either finding the bottom of the net or dishing assists to her teammates to get the job done.

Clark became the first player in WNBA history with back-to-back 30-plus-point and 10-plus-assist games. They both came in the final two games for the Fever before this international break, scoring 34 points with 12 assists in a 111-91 win over the Connecticut Sun. Then, Clark poured in 37 points, including eight of 12 three-pointers made, with 10 assists in the Aug. 23 win over the Chicago Sky, 113-90.

Clark also put together five games in August where she had at least 20 points and 10 assists. To put that into perspective, no other player had five such games in the last five seasons combined.

Finally, Clark averaged 24.4 points per game, which was the highest-scoring month by a point guard in WNBA history.

But to kick off the tournament, Lawson went with some more senior members on the squad to begin their journey to defending that gold medal. Perhaps Clark’s play will vault her into the starting lineup down the road.

Other notables who were coming off the bench for Team USA are Angel Reese and Paige Bueckers.

item.title: Gavin Newsom fires back at Trump after judge dismisses DOJ lawsuit over trans athletes in girls' sports
item.description: The Department of Justice says it will appeal after a federal judge dismissed its Title IX lawsuit against California's transgender sports policy.
item.content:encoded:
A federal judge has dismissed a Department of Justice lawsuit against California, allowing state rules that let biological males compete in girls' high school sports to remain in place. Following the ruling, Governor Gavin Newsom's office responded in a statement provided directly to OutKick.

"This ruling makes clear that President Trump cannot rewrite Title IX by fiat," a spokesperson for Newsom's office said.

"He cannot weaponize the law against the American people, and California will keep fighting his attempts to do so."

CALIFORNIA GIRLS’ SPORTS ADVOCATES VOW FIGHT AFTER JUDGE TOSSES TRANS ATHLETE CASE: 'FAR FROM OVER'

U.S. District Judge Cynthia Valenzuela never ruled on whether California’s policy violates Title IX or whether biological males should compete in girls’ sports. She tossed the case Monday, finding that federal officials failed to give California clear notice that maintaining the policy could cost the state roughly $44 billion in federal education funding.

The ruling leaves California’s policy intact for now, while the Justice Department considers an appeal.

"We are disappointed by the Court's order and remain committed to enforcing President Trump's agenda of preventing boys from playing in girls' sports," a spokesperson asserted.

The federal suit aimed to use Title IX, the landmark 1972 law created to protect female athletes, to safeguard girls' sports. But under Gov. Gavin Newsom and state athletic officials, California has maintained a 2013 policy allowing males to compete on girls’ teams.

Newsom has acknowledged on a podcast that fairness is at the heart of the debate over transgender athletes.

The Supreme Court’s recent decision upholding state bans did not create a nationwide mandate, leaving California’s policy in effect.

CALIFORNIA TRANS ATHLETE PODIUM CONTROVERSY IGNITES OUTRAGE AMONG POLITICIANS, ACTIVISTS

California’s policy drew its fiercest backlash in track and field, where Jurupa Valley High School athlete AB Hernandez won four girls’ state titles across two seasons. Hernandez captured back-to-back high jump and triple jump championships and finished third in the long jump, prompting state officials to issue duplicate medals to the girls pushed down the podium. When Hernandez later joined the girls’ varsity volleyball team, the debate moved from competitive fairness to player safety.

At least eight teams forfeited against Jurupa Valley, citing fairness and safety concerns over playing against a male competitor.

State officials point to the few trans athletes competing in California. Female athletes and advocates say even one male competitor can displace girls, alter a state championship and affect college or NIL opportunities.

With the federal case stalled, California remains a major battleground over Title IX and women’s sports.

item.title: MLW star Lady Frost reacts to Tessa Blanchard signing: 'It's good for business'
item.description: Lady Frost called Tessa Blanchard's MLW signing "incredible" and said it's good for business as the women's division continues to grow its roster.
item.content:encoded:
Pro wrestling star Tessa Blanchard signed with Major League Wrestling (MLW) earlier this week, bolstering an already stacked women’s division.

Lady Frost, who joined MLW earlier this year, reacted to Blanchard’s arrival in an interview with OutKick Dropkick.

item.title: UMass player absolutely obliterates unsuspecting woman on the sidelines after interception
item.description: UMass safety Jahmad Harmon picked off Dylan Lonergan twice as the Minutemen demolished Rutgers 37-21, snapping a 16-game FBS losing streak.
item.content:encoded:
What a start to the college football season.

For those who didn't feel like giving the big UMass-Rutgers game Thursday night your time and effort, the Minutemen stunned Greg Schiano's group, 37-21, snapping a 16-game losing streak to FBS teams.

That's right. Sixteen games. 16!

WEEK ONE UPSET SPECIAL: THESE THREE COLLEGE FOOTBALL TEAMS SHOULD BE ON UPSET ALERT THIS WEEKEND

Umass entered the night at nearly 30-point underdogs for its first defeat of an FBS program since beating Army in 2023, and it was never particularly close.

That was probably the most stunning part. The pure domination from the Minutemen from start to finish in this one was a sight to behold. UMass went into the locker room up 24-7 at the half after a 17-point second quarter, and never looked back.

As my old high school football coach used to say, it was a "good, old fashioned, country a–kicking."

And that includes on ... and OFF ... the field:

Incredible. What a scene.

That young lad would gave the old lady the unfortunate hit stick would be UMass stud safety Jahmad Harmon, for those who aren't up to date on all things Minutemen football.

HERE'S WHY, EVEN WITH ALL ITS PROBLEMS, COLLEGE FOOTBALL IS STILL BETTER THAN THE NFL

And that's all of you.

He picked off Rutgers quarterback Dylan Lonergan on the second drive of the fourth quarter, and then pulled down a second interception two drives later. The Minutemen picked off Lonergan three times Thursday night.

And before you all get nasty at me for making fun of a woman getting trucked on the sidelines ... you get what you pay for in those spots. Sorry.

Everyone knows the risks of being field-level for a football game. It's the Wild Wild West. If you're gonna stand that close to a field with 22 maniacs running around, you have to know this could always be a possibility.

This is fair game!

Anyway, UMass's stunning win was the biggest outright upset in five years (+2400), and was the program's first win versus a current power conference opponent since November 1978.

Goodness, it's good to have college football back.

item.title: Top DHS lawyer turns tables on 128 ex-judges after Bar declines ‘Worst of the Worst’ complaint
item.description: James Percival compared the 128 former judges' Florida Bar complaint to the Hunter Biden laptop controversy, calling the filing frivolous "Bar-fare."
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: DHS General Counsel James Percival is turning a complaint from 128 former judges back on its signers, calling on the Florida Bar to scrutinize those among them who are Bar members after it declined to investigate him.

The Bar said it does not investigate or prosecute sitting officers appointed under the U.S. Constitution while they are in office, a position Percival argued the complainants should have known before challenging his "Worst of the Worst Judges" series.

Percival accused the Florida Bar members who joined the complaint of potentially abusing the disciplinary process for political purposes, arguing their filing was frivolous and dubbing the tactic "Bar-fare."

"The 128 former judges are sort of an example of a tactic the left has used for a long time," Percival told Fox News Digital, comparing their appeal to professional authority to the 2020 controversy involving 51 former intelligence officials and Hunter Biden’s laptop.

DHS EVISCERATES MEDIA FOR ‘ABSOLUTE ABSURDITY’ OVER CONCERN ABOUT ‘WORST OF THE WORST’ ACTIVIST JUDGES LIST

Percival pointed to the Florida Bar's previous handling of a complaint involving former Attorney General Pam Bondi, arguing that they already signaled refusal to probe sitting presidential appointees.

"[W]hat these 128 former judges did was frivolous, and they were on notice that it was frivolous because the Florida Bar is very clear about this. So, it's ‘Bar-fare’," he said, playing on the term "lawfare."

LIBERAL LAW PROFESSOR BREAKS WITH OBAMA JUDGE OVER TRUMP LAWYER CRACKDOWN: ‘I REFUSE TO TEACH’ IT

Percival said the same tactic has been used elsewhere, including the Hunter Biden laptop controversy and the way dissent over COVID-era restrictions was met with echoes of "trust the experts."

"The left has just like often hid behind this veneer, this prestige [of expertise] and they've gotten people who carry weight to carry their water for them. And I really think the emperor has no clothes on this, but we have to call it out and expose it."

When the political left does not want to publicly debate the merits of their assertion, they get figures who appear authoritative to shut down dissent, he said.

The comments came after rule-of-law groups Democracy Defenders Fund, Lawyers Defending American Democracy and 128 former federal and state judges filed a 24-page complaint accusing Percival of violating Florida's rules governing statements about judges. The complaint alleged that Percival, a licensed Florida attorney, violated ethics rules through "public attacks on sitting judges."

"His statements mischaracterized the judges’ rulings and assailed their character and integrity. The ethics rules exist for a reason: Baseless attacks on judges by lawyers and public officials can undermine confidence in the courts and heighten the risk of physical threats against judges," Democracy Defenders Fund said in a statement after the Bar declined to investigate the complaint.

Former Florida Supreme Court Chief Justice Peggy Quince, an appointee of Democratic ex-Gov. Lawton Chiles, led the judges’ consortium.

The complaint focuses on four judges featured in Percival's "Worst of the Worst" posts, whom he accused of actions including "open defiance of the Supreme Court," "judicial sabotage" and "judicial micromanagement."

SUPREME COURT WEIGHS TRUMP EFFORT TO TERMINATE TEMPORARY PROTECTIONS FOR HAITIAN, SYRIAN MIGRANTS

The cases involved disputes over Temporary Protected Status, the government's handling of Kilmar Ábrego García and DHS use-of-force policies.

The complaint also referenced an article written by Percival condemning former President Joe Biden and a Rhode Island judge he appointed after an illegal immigrant whom DHS said had an international warrant for homicide was ordered released.

Percival said the activist judges themselves are the ones who are being a "disservice to the judiciary."

He argued that judges know their district court rulings can delay executive action when they cannot be immediately appealed.

As for the complainants, Percival said those who are themselves members of the Florida Bar should face scrutiny over whether they abused the complaint process for political purposes.

The Bar provided Fox News Digital a copy of its response sent to the Framingham, Massachusetts, address listed for the collective complainants.

Bar Counsel Christopher Wackes wrote his group does not investigate or prosecute "sitting officers appointed under the U.S. Constitution while they are in office." Wackes said any action could "encroach on the authority of the federal government."

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

He quipped situations like the bar complaint show he is over the proverbial target:

"[I]f people are this upset about what I'm doing, it must be having an effect that they don't like, which really just encourages me to keep going," he said, pressing conservatives to fight for their causes despite the knowledge the left will "try to ruin your life."

Fox News Digital's Kiera McDonald contributed to this report.

item.title: One of history's most famous battles could be rewritten by long-lost papal letter
item.description: A lost papal letter recently found in Vatican archives suggests Pope Alexander II backed William the Conqueror's invasion over England's ties to a rival pope.
item.content:encoded:
A lost letter from a pope could rewrite the story of one of history's most famous battles — nearly 1,000 years after it was fought.

The University of East Anglia announced the new research, which sheds light on the Norman Conquest of England in 1066, in August.

Professor Tom Licence was examining historical records when he came across previously overlooked excerpts from a lost papal letter that was preserved in the Vatican archives, he said.

ROYAL DECREE FROM NOTORIOUS 'SPIDER KING' REDISCOVERED IN VERY UNEXPECTED LOCATION

The letter suggests Pope Alexander II may have backed William the Conqueror's invasion of England because the English had sided with his rival — offering a new explanation for the events that led to the Battle of Hastings.

In the letter, Alexander described England as being led astray by an "evil head" and used striking religious language that Licence said branded the English as "followers of Satan."

The Battle of Hastings, one of the most consequential battles in English history, has traditionally been viewed as a fight over who had the rightful claim to the English throne: King Harold II or William of Normandy.

It has not typically been viewed as part of a broader political and religious struggle involving the papacy, but Licence said the events of 1066 may have been closely tied to a bitter power struggle between Pope Alexander II and his rival, the antipope Honorius II.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER MASSIVE ARTIFACT DEPICTING PHARAOH THOUGHT TO HAVE CHALLENGED MOSES IN EXODUS

Licence's research suggests England may have sided with Honorius, potentially giving Alexander another reason to support the Norman invasion.

Licence told Fox News Digital he wasn't personally surprised by the connection he made.

"Which papal faction England was aligning with at any given time is always in the back of my mind," the professor said.

"I suspect, however, that most historians working on the Norman Conquest are not looking at Rome that closely," he added.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER MYSTERIOUS FACE HIDDEN FOR CENTURIES IN BOOK OF REVELATION CITY

Honorius II may not be a familiar name to many — but Licence said he remained a "serious contender" in the papal power struggle, even after his position weakened in 1064.

"In fact, it looked like [Honorius II] was going to make a comeback in 1065," he said.

"Read in that context, the letter from Pope Alexander about England being led astray under an 'evil head' made sense at last. It was never clear to historians in the past what Alexander was referring to."

Licence said he was "confident" that the English moved away from backing Alexander II, which would have amounted to "a withdrawal of support."

"It's less clear to me that England openly declared support for Honorius," he said.

"Alexander's rhetoric about the English being led from the path of truth by an 'evil head' — and calling them 'followers of Satan' — suggests, at the very least, that they were leaning that way."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

He said that specializing in both fields allowed him to make the connection.

"Sometimes it just takes someone to come along and join the dots," he said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Most scholars working on the Norman Conquest aren't specialists in ecclesiastical history, and they may not, in any case, be looking closely at papal politics."

Licence said his findings change the understanding of Alexander's role in the events of 1066.

"This discovery therefore changes how we think about Alexander's motives in 1066," he said. 

"He wanted regime change in England."

The findings are detailed in Licence's new book, "Harold: Warrior King."

item.title: Even on opening weekend, football players at Clemson, LSU might be upstaged on campus by these furry friends

What if some APOCs stroll across the Quad? (APOC: that’s short for Adorable Puppies On Campus.)

While both schools may be well known for football, they’re also known for having an affinity for very special (and adorable) dogs. Both LSU and Clemson have clubs on campus that assist a national non-profit organization named Canine Companions with raising and training little puppies into full-fledged service dogs that are assigned to people in need.

Students on campus who are in the club volunteer to raise specially bred Labrador Retriever puppies for more than a year, teaching the sweet and adorable creatures commands, cues and social behavior.

So…a BMOC versus an APOC spotted in the wild on campus? Well, it might not be all that close as to which one will draw the most attention.

"When people see our dogs on campus, they always stop and say hi and ask to pet them and they’ll want to know about our club," Clemson senior Brooke Knight, president of the Canine Companions club on campus said. "They’ll want to take pictures. It’s just super cool to see people wanting to interact with us and the dogs."

The Clemson club has raised 15 dogs on campus since 2021. At LSU, the four-year-old club typically raises five dogs a year. Raisers are given approval to take their puppies to class, across campus, into every building and to events. The puppies at Clemson and LSU become part of the campus family, and, even though they are canines, they are essentially considered honorary "Tigers."

"It definitely makes you popular to walk around with a dog," said LSU sophomore and club president-elect Finley O’Con, who will be getting her first puppy to raise in about two months. "You'll talk to 15 people just walking through the quad because they want to know: ‘Why do you have a dog? What's the dog's name? Tell me about this club. Tell me about Canine Companions.’ And it's definitely really good advertisement to have a dog. "

"Raisers" undergo a comprehensive vetting process. They are typically assigned a puppy by Canine Companions around the 8-week mark of the puppy’s life, and they’ll raise the puppy for the next 14 to 16 months.

College students, typically with no other dependents, are perfect to provide the puppies with a laser focus. They also happen to be in a great environment to expose the puppies to one of the biggest parts of this stage of their learning: socialization.

From quiet libraries, in which the raisers teach their puppies to settle under a table, to bustling quads, in which the raisers teach their puppies not to chase every person or squirrel, to a gathering or loud sporting event, in which the raisers teach their puppies how to be calm amidst the chaos, college campuses challenge the puppies with every possible stimuli and circumstance.

"Through Canine Companions, it is required that (raisers) attend at least two puppy classes a month. And obviously, there are plenty of chances for the raiser to go home, teach the dog basic commands and then again, at our club meetings we like to show off their talents, and it gets the dog really excited to learn more stuff," said LSU senior Kelsey Johnson, the club’s current president. "They have a lot of different opportunities to be able to be trained. "

After about 18 months of being a raiser on campus, Clemson junior Allie McCafferty, her club’s vice president, recently returned her puppy Vinny to Canine Companions so that he could start professional training. It’s a six- to nine-month process that is the last step before a puppy can become a full-fledged service dog or facility dog.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

"He is the absolute best," McCafferty said of Vinny. "He is so incredibly calm. Nothing affects him ever. He’s so cuddly, which is my favorite. He’s incredibly attentive. Any time I look down at him, he’s just staring up at me waiting for me to tell him what to do next.

"The balance of time with classes and trying to focus on him can be a challenge. But if we are busy studying or we can’t take our dogs to a lab or something like that, we do have a lot of (dog) sitters in the club who can help us. Having the support here of the club, to watch our dogs when we need it, to have other dogs to play with, has been really great."

Of course, raisers don’t need to be college students. Raisers live all over the country, are all ages and can have all kinds of different life circumstances, from young working singles, to retired couples to busy families with multiple young kids.

Loving dogs, and wanting to help people in need, are two of the biggest criteria for raisers to become a perfect match with Canine Companions.

Canine Companions was founded in 1975 in Santa Rosa, Calif., and in 1976 the first service dog, Abdul, was placed by the organization. More than 8,500 dogs have been placed since.

Last year, the organization celebrated 50 years of service, and as of January, Canine Companions is working with more than 2,800 actively placed service dogs while guiding more than 1,100 raisers of puppies, like those at LSU and Clemson, that hope to one day be service dogs.

Over five decades, Canine Companions, at no cost to its clients, has assisted people with physical disabilities or challenges, cognitive issues and post-traumatic stress disorder. Professionals who need the assistance of the dogs as part of their work in health care, criminal justice or education also have long-standing relationships with Canine Companions.

It is this noble cause that fuels the selflessness of raisers. It can be a bittersweet job as they put so much into a beloved creature that they will ultimately have to let go.

Raisers not only devote an incredible amount of their own time and resources for more than a year while they raise the puppies into dogs that are primed for professional training, they also agree to weather the difficult emotions and tears of saying goodbye when it’s time for their puppies to move on to that next stage.

After her puppy spent nearly a year and a half with her on LSU’s campus, senior Ella Menard dropped off Loyal to professional training in May. She misses him every day.

"So Loyal's now in his second semester (at professional training), which is crazy because it feels like I just dropped him off," said Menard, the former president of the LSU club and now its current vice president. "He's moving along. He is starting to learn some ambulatory skills , like basic foundational skills for a manual wheelchair. It's exciting, He's doing fairly well.

"He's still kind of figuring out how to walk politely on a leash, which is no surprise. I fully expected that. In some outings, he's kind of, you know, getting distracted, wanting to go see everybody. He's just a very friendly dog, but he needs to focus, and I think he's getting there. He actually just got a new trainer, so we'll see how that works out. "

Interestingly, if any puppy doesn’t make it through professional training for whatever reason, raisers will be asked if they would like their puppy back, free of charge, to love again as just a pet.

Of course, all raisers hope for success, which is the bittersweet part. Success for the puppies and for the organization and for the people in need who ultimately get the dogs, means some heartache for them.

"Turning in Loyal was probably one of the hardest days of my whole life, but it taught me that I can have an attachment to something, that I can love this dog, but know that he's meant for more," Menard said. "He's going to make somebody's life a lot better. I think that's my main takeaway from the club is that you can do hard things.

"The heartbreak was hard, but the joy (Loyal) brought me was worth all the tears. "

To learn more about Canine Companions, or to donate, visit: canine.org. You may also follow Canine Companions on Instagram, Facebook and Twitter.

Would you consider being a raiser for Canine Companions, or have you been involved with the organization already? Let me know: patricia.babcockmcgraw@outkick.com.

item.title: Common cholesterol drug linked to lower dementia risk when started early
item.description: A massive study found that starting statins within a year of a type 2 diabetes diagnosis was linked to a 15% lower risk of dementia over a decade.
item.content:encoded:
Starting statin therapy shortly after a type 2 diabetes diagnosis may not only protect the heart — it may also be linked to a lower dementia risk.

A large study presented at the European Society of Cardiology Congress in Munich on Aug. 30 found that adults who began taking a statin within one year of their type 2 diabetes diagnosis had a 15% lower relative risk of developing dementia over 10 years compared to those who did not take the medication within five years.

Even for those who delayed starting a statin for one to five years, there was still a 10% lower relative risk, according to the findings, which were published in The Lancet Regional Health – Europe.

3 THINGS TO AVOID IN MIDDLE AGE COULD MEAN 13 MORE YEARS WITHOUT DEMENTIA, STUDY FINDS

A statin is a prescription medication that lowers "bad" LDL cholesterol and helps reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke.

Researchers conducted the study by tracking health data from 132,585 patients in Denmark who were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes between 2006 and 2019 and had no prior history of statin use or dementia.

During a median follow-up of 7.1 years, the team analyzed how the timing of statin treatment impacted overall dementia rates.

Dr. Liron Sinvani, a geriatrician and director for research and innovation at the Northwell Institute for Healthy Aging in New York, said this was a "well-designed, large-scale observational study that adds to a growing body of evidence suggesting that statins may help protect brain health."

GAME-CHANGING CHOLESTEROL PILL WINS FDA APPROVAL AFTER CUTTING LDL NEARLY 60%

She noted that while a 15% reduction is a modest improvement, it remains "very significant."

People with type 2 diabetes have an increased risk of cognitive decline and heart disease, consistent with previous research.

Although guidelines generally recommend statins for many adults ages 40 to 75 with diabetes, statin treatment is not always started soon after a type 2 diabetes diagnosis.

The study also examined whether the timing of treatment was linked to dementia risk. People who started statins within a year of their diagnosis had a lower risk than those who did not begin treatment.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"The message here is that maybe waiting is actually not the right approach," Sinvani said, supporting earlier consideration of statin therapy in routine diabetes care.

The expert said she found the results "especially compelling" because the benefit was driven by a lower risk of vascular dementia rather than Alzheimer's disease.

"And that makes biological sense, because we know statins lower cholesterol, reduces inflammation and protects blood vessels," she added, pointing out that these same mechanisms prevent vascular damage to the brain.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Statin therapy should be viewed as one piece of a broader health strategy alongside exercising regularly, adhering to a healthy diet and staying socially connected, according to the expert.

Almost half of dementia cases may be preventable or delayable by addressing modifiable risk factors, according to the Lancet Commission.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The study did have limitations. Because it was observational rather than a randomized clinical trial, the researchers could not definitively state that statins directly prevent dementia.

As Sinvani cautioned, "This is not proof that statins prevent dementia, but I think it's an important step in this literature."

The doctor encouraged people with type 2 diabetes who are not taking a statin to ask their doctor whether the medication is appropriate for them."

item.title: Jelly Roll picked a fight with Trump fans and may have Bud Lighted himself
item.description: Jelly Roll's Jimmy Kimmel monologue targeting Trump sparked backlash from country fans who say the move mirrors Bud Light's brand-destroying misstep.
item.content:encoded:
When country music artist Jelly Roll guest-hosted The Jimmy Kimmel Show from August 24–27 and went after President Trump, it unleashed fury from country music fans and the president’s supporters — fury sparked just in time to energize Trump voters for the midterm elections this year.

The fury at Jelly Roll isn’t because he doesn’t think like us; we tend to be free thinkers over here on the right. Rather, the big dude with all the face tattoos is — plot twist — actually not authentic at all.

And one of the things many country music fans and supporters of this president have in common is the high premium we place on authenticity. We value it, we’re loyal to it, and we can sniff out a fake.

BROADCAST BIAS: DOLLY PARTON TAUGHT THE WORLD THE WAY TO BE UNIVERSALLY BELOVED

Few people understood the value of authenticity better than the late, great Dolly Parton. She never charted a course set by someone else’s agenda just to fit in.

We don’t have to ask what she’d do if given Jimmy Kimmel’s microphone. In a 2018 ABC interview, she told us, "I learned a long time ago, keep your damn mouth shut if you want to stay in show business. I’m not in politics, I’m an entertainer."

JOHN RICH CLAIMS JELLY ROLL KNEW HE’D LOSE HALF HIS FANS OVER POLITICAL COMMENTS

That’s why America will always love Dolly, and the shelf life on Jelly is starting to stink.

Incidentally, it turns out Mr. Roll (is that the proper way to address him?) does, in fact, have a real name — Jason DeFord. However, somebody decided "Jelly" was the way to go for a 41-year-old.

Go figure.

After getting criticized for meeting with then-President-elect Trump at a UFC fight at Madison Square Garden in 2024, Jelly Roll made it a point to emphasize that he’s not political at all. He said while his parents never pushed him to vote, "they did push respecting the president though."

JELLY ROLL ROLLS AWAY FROM APOLITICAL PAST AFTER TRUMP JOKES SPARK MAGA AND ‘SNOWFLAKE’ LABELS

So excuse us for not laughing when he flipped his own script on the fans who made him famous, then pretended to be surprised we don’t get his "jokes" — and by jokes, he meant a monologue of cheap shots aimed at the president. His highlight reel included trashing the president’s poll numbers, mocking his weight — never mind that, not too long ago, there were 300 pounds of Jelly — and, of course, the left’s faithful favorite, Trump’s a racist.

Talking about the president’s appearance at the Freedom 250 Grand Prix in Washington, D.C., Jelly Roll said, "But the president seemed to enjoy the IndyCar race, which was a real switch up for him, because normally he only likes his own race."

JELLY ROLL UNLEASHES CRUDE JOKES ABOUT TRUMP'S WEIGHT ON 'KIMMEL', 'FROM ONE FAT PIG TO ANOTHER'

If liberals could start recycling some new lies, that would be great. This one’s getting old.

Surprised, or just playing the part, Jelly Roll called the backlash from fans "the weirdest thing I’ve ever done to stun people."

CHRIS ROBINSON, BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN FACE BACKLASH AS 'AMERICANS HAVE HAD ENOUGH' OF BEING LECTURED: EXPERT

Someone hand him a mirror. I think he forgot about the face tattoos.

Hollywood was watching what he’d do next, and he didn’t disappoint. He punched back at the very fans who made him a household name, telling them to delete his music.

NATALIE MAINES’ ANTI-TRUMP TIRADE, ZACH BRYAN’S FENCE-CLIMBING CLASH FUEL COUNTRY MUSIC’S BIGGEST FEUDS

As my teenagers would say, "OK, bro."

This reeks of a poser auditioning to join the cool kids club, making sure he checks all the liberal derangement boxes so they let him in.

Too bad he’ll soon find out the kids aren’t that cool, and they’ll kick you out of the club when you cease to be a useful idiot and go back to being a regular idiot.

Trump supporters have come to expect this antagonistic hostility on any day that ends in "y" from celebrities, politicians and unhinged suburban white women sipping matcha lattes in yoga pants.

We also expect authenticity. In fact, our loyalty demands it.

ROSIE O'DONNELL 'SURPRISED' BY BEING TAPPED TO GUEST HOST FOR KIMMEL, BUT EAGER FOR ANTI-TRUMP PLATFORM

People make jokes about the simplicity of country music, but authenticity is what drives the lyrics behind the music, and it’s the magnet that draws fans to the songs. That same authenticity is also what drew Trump supporters to this president.

Before President Trump shut the border, brought violent crime to a record low, brokered eight peace deals and got men out of women’s sports, it was his authenticity that first earned him unwavering support. Nearly 10 years later, it’s that same authenticity — along with his accomplishments — that’s made his supporters some of the most loyal of any president. This is something liberals, a decade later, still don’t understand.

The irony is nobody cares which bubble Jelly Roll plans to color in when he votes in November, or if he colors in any bubble at all. He, on the other hand, cares so much about appealing to a base that never knew he existed before his fans gave him a microphone that he’s willing to spit in the face of the very people who gave him the microphone.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Unless you’ve been living under a rock, you remember when Bud Light lit a match to its brand after it attempted to use a transgender influencer to sell beer to middle America. The only thing it succeeded in doing is turning its name into a verb. As in — Jelly Roll "Bud Lighted" himself.

Maybe he did. The best predictor of future behavior is past behavior, and we’ve seen this movie before.

In case anyone forgets the power of the base, in 2023, the culturally corrupt crowd crashed out over country music singer Jason Aldean’s "Try That in a Small Town," a song about small towns defending against riots and enforcing the law. They screamed "racist" until the video was pulled off Country Music Television, and they unsuccessfully attempted to bully an apology out of Aldean.

Instead, furious fans sent the song to number one on iTunes and number one on the Billboard Hot 100. Then, the next year, President Trump was re-elected. Is that the only reason? Of course not. Was his base energized after that? You bet.

Stay tuned. Jelly Roll’s four-night "truth serum" PSA could energize Republicans to get out the vote this November.

item.title: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s school warning letters reignite privacy battle they ‘cannot control’: experts
item.description: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's children Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet are reportedly starting private school in the Cotswolds, prompting warning letters to parents about privacy rules.
item.content:encoded:
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s return to the United Kingdom could become their biggest privacy test yet as their children Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet begin school life in the English countryside.

Last week, Markle, 45, and Harry, 41, along with their son Archie, 7, and daughter Princess Lilibet, 5, left their home in Montecito, California, for an extended stay in Britain.

According to reports, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex plan to settle in the Cotswolds, an affluent countryside region in south-central England, located about two hours outside London. Archie and Lilibet are reportedly set to begin classes at a private school in the U.K., though the school has not been publicly named.

PRINCE HARRY AND MEGHAN MARKLE ARRIVE IN UK WITH KIDS, MARKING DRAMATIC RETURN 6 YEARS AFTER ROYAL EXIT

In a report published Monday, royal commentator Kinsey Schofield told Page Six that parents in the Cotswolds area received warning letters from school officials after Harry and Markle "approached multiple schools" for Archie and Lilibet ahead of their move.

The letters reportedly reminded families of privacy rules surrounding students and high-profile families.

PRINCE HARRY AND MEGHAN MARKLE WON’T ‘HIJACK’ PRINCE GEORGE’S HISTORIC ETON DEBUT, ROYAL EXPERT SAYS

"The message sent to families essentially said that, from time to time, some families joining the school may attract a greater level of public or media interest," Schofield told the outlet.

The message also reportedly noted that the school wanted to preserve a "safe, happy, and private environment" for all students.

MEGHAN MARKLE’S UK RETURN POSES PALACE CONTROL ‘NIGHTMARE,’ EXPERT WARNS

"It then reminded parents and carers not to photograph or film other children without permission, or share photographs, information or details about pupils or their families on social media," Schofield said.

Page Six did not identify the school that sent the letters, citing privacy concerns, but reported that it is not the school Archie and Lilibet are attending.

PRINCE WILLIAM 'NO LONGER RECOGNIZES' PRINCE HARRY AS SECURITY BATTLE LEAVES DUKE 'CLOSE TO TEARS': EXPERT

Harry and Markle have long tried to shield their children from uncontrolled public exposure. The couple had previously skipped the traditional royal baby photo call, limited public images of their children and raised security concerns around U.K. visits.

However, royal experts told Fox News Digital that school life presents a different challenge because it places Archie and Lilibet’s privacy partly in the hands of other parents, classmates and the broader community.

PRINCE WILLIAM LIKELY 'LIVID' OVER MEGHAN MARKLE'S 'TASTELESS' PHOTOS AT PRINCESS DIANA'S HOME: EXPERT

Schofield, who also spoke to Fox News Digital about the couple’s return to Britain, said the school warnings underscore how difficult it may be for Harry and Markle to manage their children’s privacy in everyday settings.

"School introduces an enormous number of variables Harry and Meghan cannot control," the host of YouTube’s "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered" said.

"Other parents have phones. Children have friends. There are school events, sporting fixtures, birthday parties, drop-offs, and pick-ups," Schofield added. "You cannot manage a school community like a communications operation."

Schofield noted that the letter she had seen was "deliberately vague" but explained that the reminders were likely not unusual on their own. However, she argued that the attention surrounding Harry and Markle will change the dynamic for other families.

"None of those requests are unreasonable," Schofield continued. "Archie and Lili deserve exactly the same opportunity as every other child to go to school without feeling watched. But inevitably, when one family attracts this level of global attention, the entire school community becomes more conscious of what it photographs, posts, and discusses."

"Other families are effectively being asked to adjust their behavior because Harry and Meghan have arrived," she added.

PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON FACE 'SUSSEX CIRCUS' AS PRINCE GEORGE PREPARES FOR ETON: EXPERT

While speaking with Fox News Digital, royal expert Hilary Fordwich pointed out that Markle posted photos of Archie and Lilibet on her own social media, sharing her view that it was "beyond hypocritical to on the one hand want ‘privacy’ yet, on the other hand, monetize their family."

While Markle has shared photos of her children on Instagram, they are often pictured from behind, with their faces hidden or in carefully chosen images.

The former "Suits" star’s representative previously defended Markle’s approach in a statement to Newsweek.

"The Duchess has always been clear that there is a distinction between sharing moments from her life and exposing her children to public scrutiny," her spokesperson said in June. "By obscuring their faces, she is demonstrating the very principle she advocates for: giving children privacy, agency, and protection in an increasingly digital world."

Fordwich shared her view that the Sussexes’ decision to keep Archie and Lilibet largely out of public view may have had the unintended effect of making candid images more sought-after.

She contrasted the Sussexes’ approach with that of Prince William and Kate Middleton, who typically release official images of Prince George, 13, Princess Charlotte, 11, and Prince Louis, 8, on birthdays and other milestones.

"The school has a legal and moral obligation to protect their students, so it puts them likewise in a precarious position," she said.

"There will be a huge bounty regarding any resulting photos, so the incentive is there, as unlike Prince William and Catherine, who carefully release photos of their children on special occasions, the Sussexes have created this bounty situation themselves," she argued.

"Now, ordinary families have such constraints put upon them. So now they are being made subordinate to the Sussex brand."

Schofield noted that the Cotswolds has long attracted royals, celebrities and wealthy public figures seeking privacy.

Highgrove House, the country home of Harry’s father, King Charles, and Queen Camilla, is located nearby, while Princess Anne is based at Gatcombe Park.

David and Victoria Beckham, Kate Moss, Ellen DeGeneres and Portia de Rossi, Jeremy Clarkson, Hugh Grant and Elizabeth Hurley are also among the famous names who either live there full-time, keep country homes there or are frequently linked to the region.

"The Cotswolds are full of extremely wealthy and famous people precisely because discretion is part of the culture," Schofield said. "These are people who are accustomed to seeing celebrities and royals without turning it into a spectacle."

"I suspect the novelty of Harry and Meghan will wear off very quickly if their presence brings photographers, security concerns, or increased media attention," she added.

Schofield argued that the school controversy reflects a broader tension that has followed the Sussexes since they stepped back from royal duties and moved away from the U.K. in 2020.

"Privacy was one of the central themes surrounding their departure, and six years later they have returned to Britain and almost immediately we are talking about privacy again," she said.

"But there is an important distinction between reasonable privacy and control," Schofield continued. "Harry and Meghan are entitled to protect their children, their home and genuinely private moments. Where they have struggled historically is accepting that privacy does not necessarily mean controlling every headline, photograph, or public conversation about them."

"If they want this move to work, they may have to develop a much higher tolerance for things they cannot control," Schofield added.

Schofield suggested that Harry and Markle consider emulating the example set by William and Middleton.

"I do think Harry should look at how William and Catherine have navigated this," she said. "Their children have grown up under extraordinary scrutiny, yet the Waleses have established boundaries with the media while accepting that public interest comes with their children’s unique position."

The Sussexes’ desire to reconnect with Charles and other members of the royal family has been reported as one of the reasons behind their move back to the U.K.
